records.sourceFile: Statistical analysis and machine learning in college football - Insights from offensive efficiency, yards per play, and clustering play styles.pdf

paper.citation: Salloum SA, Aljanada RA, Alhumaid K, Alomari KM, Alfaisal AM, Elnekiti A, et al. Statistical Analysis and Machine Learning in College Football: Insights from Offensive Efficiency, Yards Per Play, and Clustering of Play Styles. In: Al-Marzouqi A, et al., eds. Generative AI in Creative Industries. Studies in Computational Intelligence 1208. Springer; 2025. p. 433-446.
paper.abstract: This study used team-level college football statistics from 2013 to 2023 to examine which offensive and defensive metrics relate to wins and score margins, and to cluster teams by play style. The authors report that offensive efficiency and yards per play were the strongest predictors of wins, that three play-style clusters emerged, and that a Random Forest model predicted score margins with an RMSE of 6.82.
paper.tldr: Team-level data suggest that offensive efficiency and yards per play are associated with winning in college football. The clusters and score-margin model are descriptive, and the predictors overlap, so they do not show which tactics would improve a specific team.
paper.methods: Secondary dataset of college football team statistics (2013 to 2023) was cleaned, aggregated and standardised. Offensive efficiency (total yards divided by plays) and turnover margin were derived. The analysis used descriptive rankings, a correlation matrix with wins, OLS regression on wins, K-Means clustering with three clusters on standardised offensive efficiency and yards per play, and Random Forest regression for score margin with feature importance.
paper.findings: The top-ranked team by offensive efficiency was Oklahoma (6.85 yards per play), and efficiency showed a rising trend over the decade. Correlations with wins were highest for total points (0.83) and losses (-0.82, negative). In OLS, offensive efficiency and yards per play each had a coefficient of 1.310 (p < 0.001), R-squared was 0.381, and turnover margin was not significant (p = 0.956). The Random Forest model had RMSE 6.82, with offensive efficiency (0.405) and yards per play (0.373) ranked highest. Note: Table 3 and Table 4 show identical values for offensive efficiency and yards per play, which the authors do not explain.
paper.limitations: Offensive efficiency and yards per play are calculated the same way in this paper, so the regression and clustering double-count one measure. The number of team-seasons and out-of-sample validation of the regression are not reported, missing values were filled with means, and total points is partly determined by winning. The authors note the absence of player, weather, opponent and coaching data, and that K-Means assumes clusters of similar shape and size.
paper.practicalImplications: Football performance and analytics staff can use team-level efficiency benchmarks as a broad reference point when reviewing season data. Any change in play style should be tested against the team's own data and opponent context, because this study does not establish cause and effect.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff may find the team-level efficiency framing useful for reviewing offensive output across a season. The paper does not measure individual athletes, so it cannot support player development decisions.
paper.rtp: This paper does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot be used for return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Is extensive cardiopulmonary screening useful in athletes with previous asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.pdf

paper.citation: Gervasi SF, Pengue L, Damato L, Monti R, Pradella S, Pirronti T, et al. Is extensive cardiopulmonary screening useful in athletes with previous asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection? Br J Sports Med. 2020;0:1-8.
paper.abstract: This cohort study screened professional soccer players who had asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection with a comprehensive protocol including blood tests, spirometry, resting and stress ECG, and echocardiogram. The authors compared findings with pre-infection data and with uninfected players. None of the infected players had significant cardiovascular abnormalities after recovery, although spirometry values fell significantly in the infected group. The authors conclude that extensive cardiorespiratory and haematological screening appears unnecessary in athletes with asymptomatic or mild infection.
paper.tldr: In a small group of professional soccer players with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19, a full cardiorespiratory screen found no significant heart abnormalities after recovery. Routine extended screening appears unnecessary in this group, though a raised troponin should prompt cardiac MRI and a return to training only after normalisation.
paper.methods: Cohort study of 30 male professional soccer players at one centre, screened with the Italian FIGC protocol for resuming training. Players were grouped by serology and swab results into COVID-19 positive (IgG positive, n = 18, mild or asymptomatic) and negative (n = 12). Assessments included personal history, blood tests, spirometry, resting and stress ECG with oxygen saturation, echocardiogram, 24-hour Holter, and chest CT in the positive group. Comparisons used Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests, with pre-infection data available for a subset (15 positive and 9 negative players).
paper.findings: After recovery, no significant differences were found between infected and uninfected players in spirometry, stress ECG or echocardiogram. Within the infected group (n = 15 with prior data), absolute FVC, FEV1, PEF and MVV and the percent-predicted values for FEV1, PEF and MVV fell significantly (p < 0.05; FVC percent predicted p = 0.18), and resting HR rose from 53 to 65 bpm; uninfected players showed non-significant falls. Values stayed in the normal range except two players with mildly reduced PEF, and one player with raised troponin I had normal ECG, echocardiogram, Holter, CT and cardiac MRI, with troponin normalising after 4 weeks.
paper.limitations: The study had a small, single-centre sample of male professional soccer players, no longitudinal follow-up, and no pre-infection troponin or Holter data. Cardiac MRI was performed in only one player, and the authors attribute the spirometry fall to detraining rather than infection, a hypothesis supported only by a later retest. Pre-infection comparisons were available for only 24 of 30 players.
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19, the authors suggest that history, swab and antibody testing followed by routine preparticipation screening may be sufficient in most cases, with a more cautious approach for raised troponin or abnormal echocardiogram or stress ECG. Chest CT was judged unnecessary for screening, and Holter was not needed routinely when resting and stress ECGs were normal. Raised troponin should prompt contrast cardiac MRI and a pause in training until levels normalise.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should expect some drop in spirometry and a higher resting heart rate after a training interruption, which the authors attribute to detraining. Retesting after a month of retraining is one practical check, since most measures improved in this cohort.
paper.rtp: The paper gives a return-to-training approach for athletes after mild or asymptomatic COVID-19: a standard screen is enough unless troponin or cardiac findings are abnormal. Abnormal troponin should be followed by cardiac MRI and training should resume only after troponin normalises, with clinical follow-up. Findings come from one cohort, so they should be applied with a physician's clinical judgement.

records.sourceFile: On the predictive validity of the National Football League combine - Does it forecast future success.pdf

paper.citation: Rishis E, Johnston K, Baker J. On the predictive validity of the National Football League combine: does it forecast future success? J Sports Sci. 2023.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review synthesised peer-reviewed studies on whether NFL Combine measures predict future success. Of 1,954 records, 68 studies were retained, covering medical testing, combine tests, draft position, career longevity, salary and playing performance. The authors found mixed results across combine measures, and concluded that more research is needed on long-term performance.
paper.tldr: NFL combine results, particularly the 40-yard dash, are consistently associated with draft position, but evidence that they predict later NFL performance is mixed. Prior injuries such as ACL reconstruction were linked to worse draft position and fewer games, but evidence on career length is limited and inconsistent.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA. Five databases (EconLit, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Sports Medicine and Education Index, Web of Science) were searched with 'combine' combined with 'sport' or 'NFL', with reference-list searching. Full-text peer-reviewed articles that examined NFL combine measures against at least one future outcome were included, and studies were coded by outcome, sample size and position. Coding reliability was checked on 103 articles (100% agreement).
paper.findings: Medical testing and future performance was the largest group (25 studies), followed by combine tests (12), draft position (10) and draft plus future performance (8). All 10 draft-position studies reported that a faster 40-yard dash was associated with better draft selection. ACL injury and reconstruction were associated with worse draft pick, fewer games and lower snap percentage, but one career-length study found isolated ACL reconstruction did not shorten mean career length while meniscectomy and combined ACL and meniscal surgery did; results for jumps, the 20-yard shuttle, the 3-cone drill and the Wonderlic test were mixed.
paper.limitations: The review included only peer-reviewed articles, so information shared through websites, media and other non-peer-reviewed sources was excluded. Different measures of success across studies prevented statistical comparison, and the authors note far more studies on offensive than defensive positions. No pooled estimates or study quality appraisal are reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Scouts and performance staff can treat the 40-yard dash and its split times as the best-supported combine measure for draft-related decisions, while recognising that its link to later performance is uncertain. Injury history such as ACL reconstruction, Lisfranc injury or rotator cuff repair was linked to worse draft and early-career outcomes, but the review does not support using combine results alone as a predictor of NFL success.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff working with college prospects, the review suggests that the 40-yard dash and split times relate to draft outcomes, but combine scores should not be read as a reliable forecast of long-term NFL playing performance.
paper.rtp: The review gives limited guidance on return to sport. It reports conflicting evidence after ACL reconstruction: one study found no loss of functional athletic performance in fully recovered players, while another found lower snap percentage, and career-length data exist only for linemen. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Predicting severity of head collision events in elite soccer using preinjury data - A machine learning approach.pdf

paper.citation: Tarzi G, Tarzi C, Saha A, Cusimano MD. Predicting Severity of Head Collision Events in Elite Soccer Using Preinjury Data: A Machine Learning Approach. Clin J Sport Med. 2023;33(2):165-171.
paper.abstract: This study built machine learning models to predict the severity of head collision events in elite soccer from 23 preinjury variables. Data came from 263 events across four elite international tournaments. Models reached an average AUC of 0.73 for men's tournaments and 0.70 for combined men's and women's tournaments. Injury mechanism and the event before injury were the most important predictors.
paper.tldr: In elite international soccer, head collisions after corner kicks and throw-ins were more often severe, and head-to-head plus knee-to-head contact was linked to severity in men's matches only. A random forest model using pre-injury factors classified severity with modest cross-validated accuracy (AUC 0.70 to 0.73).
paper.methods: Head collision events (direct head contact with the player unable to resume play within 5 seconds) were previously coded by 12 trained reviewers, with two reviewers independently analyzing each of 231 matches; an event was severe when the player showed more than 2 visible concussion signs. Random forest classification with nested cross-validation (100 iterations of 4-fold outer CV) was run on a male dataset (23 predictors) and a mixed male and female dataset (20 predictors), and Fisher exact tests assessed associations with severity.
paper.findings: The male dataset (215 HCEs) had a mean AUC of 0.73 and the mixed dataset (263 HCEs) a mean AUC of 0.70. Head-to-head plus knee-to-head mechanisms were associated with severity in the male dataset (P=0.0244) but not the mixed dataset (P=0.1113). Corner kicks plus throw-ins were associated with severity in both datasets (male P=0.0001; mixed P=0.0004).
paper.limitations: Severity reflects signs seen on video, not a medical diagnosis. Only 6 severe events occurred in women's matches, so no separate women's model was built. Performance was estimated by internal cross-validation only, with no external validation. The mechanism association disagreed between the male and mixed datasets. Camera angles could limit coding, and elite international data may not generalize.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff and officials could give closer attention to players involved in head-to-head or knee-to-head contact, and to head collisions after corner kicks and throw-ins, which were more often severe in this dataset. Use this as a prompt for assessment, not as a validated screening tool.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not inform athlete development or performance training. Its findings concern the severity of head collision events in elite soccer.
paper.rtp: It can support a cautious decision to assess players promptly after head-to-head or knee-to-head contact, or after a head collision from a corner kick or throw-in. It cannot determine whether an individual athlete can return to play, because severity was coded from video and the model was not validated for individual prediction.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing NFL Draft Selections with Machine Learning Classification.pdf

paper.citation: Enaganti A, Pappas G. Optimizing NFL Draft Selections with Machine Learning Classification. AI. 2025;6:221.
paper.abstract: This study used machine learning, mainly random forest models, to predict NFL draft selections and simulate drafts under best-player-available and need-based strategies. Need-based drafting produced a lower mean absolute error and higher Top-3 accuracy against the real 2017 first round. The authors present the simulator as a decision-support tool for teams.
paper.tldr: A random forest model can predict where draft prospects are picked and, in a simulation of the 2017 first round, a need-based strategy matched real picks more closely than a best-player-available strategy. These results describe agreement with actual draft outcomes, not proof of better long-term player performance.
paper.methods: Public ESPN draft prospect data were merged and drafts from 1967 to 2010 removed. A random forest regressor used four inputs (position, draft grade, position rank, overall rank) to predict pick number, trained on 2016 to 2019 drafts and tested on the 2020 class, and was compared with a decision tree and a linear support vector machine. Draft simulations applied best-player-available and need-based rules to the 2017 first round, scored by mean absolute error and a partial-credit Top-3 score against the real picks.
paper.findings: The four-input random forest reached a Pearson correlation of 0.94 and RMSPE of 0.41 on the 2020 test set, better than the decision tree and support vector machine. Adding height and weight lowered the correlation, and a text-derived grade also performed worse. For the simulated 2017 first round, need-based drafting had MAE 6.7 and a Top-3 score of 77.5, compared with MAE 8.8 and 71.9 for best-player-available, which matched the exact slot and team for 12.5% of picks.
paper.limitations: Validation uses one draft year, and the need-based weighting parameter was tuned on the same comparison. The paper does not state which training years fed the 2017 simulation, so overlap between training data and the simulated draft cannot be ruled out. Trades were not modeled, and the authors note that real draft outcomes may not reflect optimal picks; later NFL performance was not measured. The abstract's claims about beating conventional methods and judging which picks were more impactful are not tested in the results. Top-3 is reported as 77.4 in one place and 77.5 in another, and Tables 7 and 10 report identical values for different models.
paper.practicalImplications: Front offices could use a simulator like this to anticipate which prospects are likely to be available at their pick. Its value for evaluating prospects is unproven, so it should sit alongside scouting and not replace it.
paper.athleteDev: The study is about draft selection modeling rather than training or athlete development. It offers a possible way to forecast draft positions, which may inform recruitment and roster planning rather than how athletes develop.
paper.rtp: This study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Prospective validation of 2B-Cool - Integrating wearables and individualized predictive analytics to reduce heat injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Laxminarayan S, Hornby S, Belval LN, Giersch GEW, Morrissey MC, Casa DJ, et al. Prospective Validation of 2B-Cool: Integrating Wearables and Individualized Predictive Analytics to Reduce Heat Injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023;55(4):751-764.
paper.abstract: The authors prospectively tested 2B-Cool, a wearable and smartphone system that estimates core body temperature and predicts it 20 minutes ahead to warn of rising heat strain. In a controlled chamber study of 22 young adults across four heat and clothing conditions, core temperature estimates tracked rectal measurements closely, and the early-warning system gave useful lead time before a 38.50 C threshold.
paper.tldr: A smartwatch and smartphone system estimated core temperature within about 0.45 C of rectal measurements during 7.5-hour heat stress trials in a chamber. Its early warning for 38.50 C gave roughly 35 minutes of lead time, but this has only been shown in a laboratory.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover chamber study in which 22 healthy young adults (11 men, 11 women) completed up to four 7.5-hour trials, varying clothing (T-shirt and shorts or combat uniform) and environment (30 C at 60% humidity or 36 C at 30% humidity), with three treadmill work bouts per trial. Core temperature was measured by rectal probe; 82 of 88 trials were analyzed. Agreement was assessed with bias, MAE, RMSE, MAPE, correlation, and Bland-Altman limits, and early-warning performance with sensitivity, specificity, prediction horizon and false alarm rate.
paper.findings: Across 82 trials, core temperature estimates had mean bias 0.16 C (SD 0.34), MAE 0.39 C, RMSE 0.45 C, and Pearson r 0.89, meeting the authors' bias criterion of less than 0.27 C. The 20-minute predictions had RMSE 0.56 C, with 73% (SD 19%) of measurements inside the 95% prediction interval. For a 38.50 C threshold the early warning had sensitivity 98%, specificity 81%, a 36-minute effective horizon and 0.12 false alarms per hour; for 39.20 C, sensitivity was 87%, specificity 77% and 0.35 false alarms per hour, so specificity at both thresholds and sensitivity at 39.20 C fell short of the authors' preset 90% criterion. No sex differences were found in measured or estimated peak temperature or in warning performance.
paper.limitations: Testing was limited to 22 healthy young adults in a controlled chamber with one treadmill protocol, and field validation is still needed. The smoothing step means the system cannot follow temperature changes faster than about 10 minutes, so performance in stop-and-go sports such as American football is unknown, and it cannot detect hypothermia or non-exertional temperature rises. Figures differ between sections: nearly 75% versus 73% within the prediction interval, a 35 versus 36 minute horizon, and 81% versus 80% specificity. Two authors (S. L. and J. R.) receive royalties for licensing 2B-Cool.
paper.practicalImplications: A wrist wearable with individualized modeling tracked rectal temperature to within about 0.4 C on average and flagged most rises above 38.50 C roughly 35 minutes ahead in steady chamber exercise. Expect false alerts given the 77% to 81% specificity, and do not treat an alert or its absence as a substitute for rectal temperature when exertional heat illness is suspected.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure training adaptation or performance. It shows only that core temperature during long, steady exercise in the heat can be estimated from wrist-worn heart rate, skin temperature and activity data.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport after heat illness or any injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return to activity.

records.sourceFile: Concurrent validity and test-retest reliability of VALD ForceDecks strength, balance, and movement assessment tests.pdf

paper.citation: Collings TJ, Lima YL, Dutaillis B, Bourne MN. Concurrent validity and test-retest reliability of VALD ForceDecks strength, balance, and movement assessment tests. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: The authors compared portable uniaxial VALD ForceDecks plates with laboratory force plates for common strength, balance and movement tests in 16 healthy adults tested twice. Vertical force and centre of pressure agreed closely, and most discrete metrics showed good or excellent validity and reliability. Reliability was similar between the two systems.
paper.tldr: Portable ForceDecks plates recorded vertical force and centre of pressure very close to laboratory plates during strength, balance and jump tests. Most metrics were reliable between days, but this depended on the specific test and metric and on strict testing procedures.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures study with 16 healthy physically active adults (10 men, 6 women) tested on two sessions about 7 days apart. Twelve standard ForceDecks tests were recorded simultaneously on stacked portable and laboratory force plates. Raw time series were compared using RMSE and Bland-Altman analysis, discrete metrics by percentage difference, and test-retest reliability by ICC, SEM and minimal detectable change over 3 trials.
paper.findings: Median RMSE for vertical force ranged from 2.5 to 25.2 N, and mean bias was -2 to -1 N, with limits of agreement from -6 to 3 N. Centre of pressure bias was -0.1 to 0.0 mm. Of 674 validity metrics, about 79% had good or excellent validity (abstract figure 530/674), and about 79% of 773 metrics had good or excellent reliability (ICC above 0.75). Shoulder isometric I, T and Y metrics had the weakest agreement, and quiet-stand COP metrics had poor reliability (ICC 0.21 to 0.43). ForceDecks reliability was similar to the laboratory plates, with median ICC differences below 0.07.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and included healthy active adults, not elite athletes. Stacking the plates may have affected the laboratory readings, and time-window alignment was imperfect. The results apply to ForceDecks' own analysis methods. Reliability was based on two sessions. The abstract reports 611 of 773 reliable metrics, while the results report 385 excellent plus 228 good, which is 613. The study was funded by VALD, and several authors have relationships with VALD, which is disclosed.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners can use ForceDecks for vertical force and centre of pressure measurement when protocols are strictly standardized. Check each test and metric's validity and reliability before using it to detect change, since COP balance metrics and shoulder isometric rate of force development were weaker. Repeat a test if protocol errors are suspected.
paper.athleteDev: The study supports using portable force plates to track jump, strength and balance performance over time. Judge change against each metric's minimal detectable change in Table 1 rather than treating any between-session difference as real.
paper.rtp: The tests may help monitor strength, balance and jump metrics during rehabilitation, but the study used healthy adults and did not assess injured participants or return-to-sport criteria. Use the reliability values only as a guide to detectable change and do not use the study to set clearance thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Measurement properties of upper extremity physical performance tests in athletes - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Barbosa GM, Calixtre LB, Fialho HRF, Locks Neto F, Kamonseki DH. Measurement properties of upper extremity physical performance tests in athletes: a systematic review. Braz J Phys Ther. 2023:100575.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarized the reliability, measurement error and validity of upper extremity physical performance tests used with athletes. Fifteen studies with 684 athletes covered 13 tests, and the authors graded the quality of evidence for each property. The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test showed sufficient reliability, while most other tests had insufficient or unclear evidence.
paper.tldr: The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test have the strongest reliability evidence for athletes (moderate to high quality for the CKCUEST, moderate for the shot-put). Validity, measurement error and responsiveness evidence is thin or missing for nearly all upper extremity tests.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with a prospective registration (CRD42021241883). Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, CENTRAL, SCOPUS, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched to July 2022. Two reviewers rated study quality with the COSMIN checklist, and evidence was graded by measurement property using adapted Terwee criteria. Included studies assessed upper extremity tests in athletes of any sport and level.
paper.findings: The CKCUEST had sufficient inter-session reliability (ICC 0.79 to 0.93, moderate quality of evidence) and sufficient intra-session reliability (ICC 0.86 to 0.95, high quality), but insufficient validity against isokinetic rotator strength (r 0.55 to 0.59, low quality). The seated single-arm shot-put test had sufficient inter-session reliability (ICC 0.92 to 0.94, moderate quality) and sufficient validity in one study (r 0.73 to 0.83, low quality). The seated medicine ball throw showed insufficient validity against Wingate peak power (r 0.40 to 0.54, moderate quality). Most other tests had low quality evidence, and measurement error could not be rated because minimal important change has not been defined.
paper.limitations: Primary studies were small, often rated doubtful in methodological quality, and none reported responsiveness or minimal important change. About 70% of participants were men, and technology-dependent instruments such as dynamometers and motion analysis were excluded. The paper is internally inconsistent: the Conclusion says the CKCUEST and repetition to failure assessment showed sufficient validity, but the results rate both insufficient (r 0.55 to 0.59 and 0.20 to 0.40), and the Implications for Practice call the seated medicine ball throw valid although the results rate its validity insufficient. The abstract gives the search date as March 2021, but the Methods say searches ran to July 2022.
paper.practicalImplications: The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test appear reproducible enough for clinical use with athletes, based on reliability evidence. Use the seated medicine ball throw for upper body power only with caution, given the insufficient validity evidence. Treat other upper extremity tests as unproven, and when re-testing, keep the interval, setting and instructions consistent across sessions.
paper.athleteDev: The CKCUEST and the seated shot-put test may be used to track upper body stability and power over time, but changes should be compared against each test's measurement error, which is often missing. The review does not address how these tests relate to training outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review notes that PPTs are used to guide rehabilitation progress and return to play, but it finds too little evidence on responsiveness, measurement error and validity to support clearance decisions. Use the CKCUEST and seated shot-put tests as reliable measures only, and do not rely on the other tests to decide when an athlete can return.

records.sourceFile: The validity and reliability of commercially available resistance training monitoring devices - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Weakley J, Morrison M, García-Ramos A, Johnston R, James L, Cole MH. The Validity and Reliability of Commercially Available Resistance Training Monitoring Devices: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined the validity and reliability of commercial portable devices that measure force, velocity and power during resistance training. Forty-four studies were included, and the authors found that linear transducers were generally the most accurate, while accelerometers, smartphone apps and optic devices showed more variable error. Most validity studies lacked a gold-standard criterion measure, and many reliability studies did not separate device error from human variability.
paper.tldr: Linear position transducers gave the most accurate and reproducible velocity data in this review. Accelerometers, smartphone apps and optic devices showed more error, particularly with heavy loads, and much of the evidence lacks a gold-standard comparison.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching SPORTDiscus, Web of Science and Medline in August 2020, with reference-list screening. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language original research on the validity or reliability of portable commercial devices during resistance training. Reporting quality was rated with a nine-item modified Downs and Black checklist. Acceptable validity was defined as r above 0.70, CV below 10% and effect size below 0.60, and acceptable reliability as ICC at least 0.90, CV below 10% and standardized bias below 0.60.
paper.findings: Of 44 studies, 36 assessed validity and 28 assessed reliability. Linear transducers had the highest accuracy, but most accelerometer validity studies compared devices against other devices rather than gold-standard motion capture. Accelerometer CVs typically ranged from 10% to 20%, and mean velocity at loads above 90% of 1RM had CVs of about 27% to 35%. Smartphone and tablet apps showed substantial bias and error across devices and users. The Flex optic laser showed acceptable validity for mean velocity across 20% to 100% of 1RM, with typical error around 0.02 m/s from 40% to 100% of 1RM. Mean study reporting quality was 8.0 of 9 (SD 1.3).
paper.limitations: The search used three databases and English-language studies only, with reference-list searches added. Most included studies were small and focused on the squat and bench press, in free-weight or Smith machine form, and few tested Olympic weightlifting. Many validity studies lacked a gold-standard criterion, and most reliability studies did not separate technological from biological variation. Statistical reporting was often incomplete, which limited the comparison of devices.
paper.practicalImplications: Where accurate barbell velocity matters, linear transducers have the strongest evidence in this review. The authors suggest accelerometers are best kept for motivational feedback during ballistic, high-velocity exercises and should not be used to track performance changes or to set loads or set volume with velocity loss thresholds. Smartphone apps need thorough user familiarisation and standardised protocols because bias and error vary across devices and users.
paper.athleteDev: Validated velocity monitoring can support load prescription and feedback during resistance training, which may help plan athlete development. The review advises against using accelerometers to track changes in performance or to set loads and volume, so the choice of device should match the purpose.
paper.rtp: The review covers healthy resistance training devices and does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It does not support using these devices to make return-to-play clearance decisions.
